title: A Pile Is a Load Path You Cannot See
summary: A deep foundation carries a building's weight past weak ground into soil or rock that can hold it, through friction along the pile and bearing at its tip. Because nobody can see the finished pile, the whole discipline rests on evidence: test piles, load tests and a record of every pile installed. Learn the load path and the evidence, and you can ask the right questions of any foundation design.
body:
A pile is a column buried in the ground that carries the building past soil that cannot hold it, and because you will never see it again once it is installed, everything you know about it comes from the evidence you insisted on collecting while it went in.

Recall

Q. In a geotechnical report, what is the difference between bearing capacity and settlement?

A. Bearing capacity is the pressure the soil can take before it fails in shear. Settlement is how far the foundation moves down under the load it actually carries. A footing can be safe in bearing and still settle too much, and settlement usually governs.

Q. What does a site logistics plan show?

A. Where cranes, hoists, deliveries, laydown, site offices, haul routes and pedestrian protection sit at each stage of the build, so that the site works as a machine rather than a crowd.

Q. What is a lateral system in a building?

A. The set of elements, such as shear walls, braced frames or moment frames, that carries wind and earthquake forces sideways through the structure and down to the foundation.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, last week Greta taught you to read a geotechnical report for shallow foundations: footings and mats that spread load into the ground just below the building. This week the report says something harder. The upper soil is too soft, too loose, too variable or too compressible to carry the building, so the load must travel down through it to a layer that can. That decision changes the budget, the schedule, the risk register and the contract. Deep foundations are often one of the largest single subcontracts on a mid-rise building on poor ground, and they are the first major work in the ground, which means every day they run long delays every trade after them.

They are also the work you can verify least. A column you can measure, photograph and test for years. A pile disappears the day it is finished. So your job as owner is not to design piles. It is to make sure the design rests on enough ground information, that test results confirm the design before production starts, and that every pile installed has a record you could defend in a courtroom ten years later.

How a pile carries load

In plain English: a pile holds up the building in two ways. The soil grips its sides, and the soil or rock under its tip pushes back.

The professional framing names these two parts. Skin friction, also called shaft resistance, is the resistance mobilised along the side of the pile as it tries to slide down past the soil. End bearing is the resistance at the tip. A pile driven into deep dense sand may carry most of its load in friction. A pile socketed into rock may carry most of it in end bearing. Most piles carry a mix, and the mix matters, because friction is mobilised with very small movement while full end bearing needs more movement at the tip.

Applied example, with hypothetical round numbers. A geotechnical engineer estimates that a pile will develop 360 kips of skin friction along its length and 180 kips of end bearing, for an ultimate capacity of 540 kips. A kip is 1,000 pounds of force. Applying a factor of safety of 2, chosen by the engineer under the governing code and the testing planned, the allowable load is 270 kips per pile. A column delivering 2,000 kips to its pile cap needs at least 8 piles at that allowable load before any other effect is considered. The factor of safety is not padding. It covers soil variability, installation quality and the uncertainty of the method, and a stronger testing programme can sometimes justify a lower one.

The pile families and what each risks

Driven piles, such as precast concrete, steel H-piles and steel pipe, are hammered into the ground. Driving displaces and densifies soil, and the blow count during the final few feet tells you something about capacity on every single pile. The risks are noise, vibration that can damage neighbours, and piles that refuse early on a boulder or run long into soft ground.

Drilled shafts, also called caissons or bored piles, are excavated and filled with reinforcing steel and concrete. They can be large and carry heavy loads with few elements. Their risk is what you cannot see: a collapsed hole, a soft bottom, a void or a soil inclusion in the concrete. They depend on inspection of the hole and integrity testing afterwards.

Augercast or continuous flight auger piles are drilled with a hollow auger and grouted as the auger is withdrawn. They are quiet and fast. Their quality lives in the rig's monitoring data: grout volume against hole volume, and the rate of auger withdrawal. Micropiles and helical piles are small-diameter options for tight sites, retrofits and light loads.

No family is best. The right one depends on the soil profile, the loads, the neighbours, the water table, local contractor experience and the testing you can afford. Ask the geotechnical engineer which families were considered and why the others were rejected.

Say that out loud now.

Downdrag: when the ground pulls the pile down

In plain English: if a soft layer near the surface settles after the piles go in, it can hang on the piles and drag them down instead of holding them up.

The professional term is downdrag, or negative skin friction. It happens when fill is placed over soft clay, when the water table is lowered, or when a soft layer is still consolidating under its own weight. The settling soil adds load to the pile rather than resisting it.

Applied example, again hypothetical. On the same pile, the top 20 feet pass through soft clay that will settle under new site fill. The pile's perimeter is 6 feet, and the engineer estimates negative friction of 0.5 ksf, meaning kips per square foot, in that layer. The drag load is 0.5 times 6 times 20, which is 60 kips. That clay also no longer contributes positive friction. If the design ignored it, the pile is carrying 60 kips it was never sized for, and the positive friction it was counted on to provide in those 20 feet never arrives. The answer may be longer piles, a coating that reduces friction in the soft layer, or a change in how much fill is placed. Each has a cost, which is why downdrag has to be found in design, not discovered in year three.

How the best do it

Leading contractors and owners on large foundation jobs commonly run an indicator or test pile programme before production: a few piles installed with the production rig, instrumented, load tested and sometimes exhumed or cored, with the results used to confirm length and driving or drilling criteria for every pile after them. What a small developer can copy is the sequence, not the scale. Put the test programme in the contract, put its results on the critical path, and do not let production piling start until the geotechnical engineer has signed off the criteria in writing.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating the foundation as a quantity to buy rather than a hypothesis to prove. The design length is a prediction from a handful of borings. The control is a testing and record regime: test piles first, criteria confirmed, every production pile logged against those criteria, and any pile that departs from them flagged to the engineer the same day.

The beginner's mistake

Choosing the pile family, or the contractor, on price per foot alone. A cheaper pile that needs twice the testing, or that the local market installs poorly, is not cheaper. Compare installed, tested and documented cost per kip of reliable capacity.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: foundation costs are capitalised into the building rather than expensed; ask your tax adviser how they are classed for depreciation, and verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: piles that settle years later create claims against the owner first, so the contracts must pass that risk to the designers and installers who controlled it. Banking: the lender's monitor will want the test programme and pile records before releasing foundation draws. Governance: any change to the pile design should be an owner decision logged with the engineer's reasoning. Estate: a building with a documented foundation is an easier asset for heirs to hold or sell. Exit: a buyer's engineer will ask for pile records, and a missing record lowers the price.

Callback

In Week 103, Bram taught that every building is a load path from roof to ground, and that a path is only as strong as its weakest link. This week finishes that path. The pile is the last link, and the one link you cannot inspect after the fact, so the evidence you gather during installation is the inspection.

Recap

A pile carries load through skin friction and end bearing, sized with a factor of safety the engineer must justify. Each pile family carries a different installation risk. Downdrag can turn resisting soil into added load. Test first, then produce, and record every pile.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: the Millennium Tower settlement.
checklist: I have asked which pile families were considered and why the others were rejected.
I know how the design splits capacity between skin friction and end bearing.
I know the factor of safety used and what testing it assumes.
I have asked whether any layer can cause downdrag, and how the design handles it.
Production piling cannot start until the test results and criteria are signed off.
Every production pile will be logged against written acceptance criteria.
I compare pile options on installed, tested and documented cost per kip.
Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineer and structural engineer of record.
head: Field checklist
speak: A pile is a buried column that carries the building past weak soil into ground that can hold it. It works two ways: skin friction along its sides and end bearing at its tip. The engineer adds the two, applies a factor of safety, and gets an allowable load per pile. In a hypothetical case, 360 kips of friction and 180 of end bearing give 540 ultimate, 270 allowable at a factor of 2, so a 2,000 kip column needs at least 8 piles. Then I ask about downdrag: if a soft layer settles after installation, it hangs on the pile and adds load instead of resisting it. Because I will never see a pile again once it is in, the evidence is the inspection. So test piles go first, the criteria are signed off before production, and every pile is logged against them. I buy proven capacity, not feet of pile.
terms: Skin friction — the resistance the soil provides along the side of a pile as it tries to move down, also called shaft resistance.
End bearing — the resistance provided by the soil or rock directly under the tip of a pile.
Downdrag — added downward load on a pile from a settling soil layer around it, also called negative skin friction.

hostile.q: Your pile budget assumes 60-foot piles from four borings across a large site. What happens to my loan if they run to 90 feet?
hostile.a: Then the foundation line grows and the schedule moves, and I would rather you hear how we control that now than discover it at draw time. Before production we install and load test indicator piles with the production rig, and the geotechnical engineer confirms the length and acceptance criteria in writing. The contract pays for pile length on unit rates with an agreed quantity range, so extra length has a known price, and I carry a foundation-specific contingency sized to the length range the borings support. If the test piles show a longer design, I re-run the cost to complete and the in-balance test before we drive the first production pile.

title: Millennium Tower: A Foundation That Stopped Short
summary: A tall residential tower in San Francisco, completed in 2009 on friction piles that ended in dense sand rather than bedrock, was publicly reported in 2016 to have settled and tilted well beyond what was expected. Seven forensic steps show how a defensible design choice became a decade of litigation and a costly retrofit. The lesson is about long-term settlement, neighbours and evidence.
body:
The Millennium Tower in San Francisco was finished in 2009 on piles that stopped in sand above bedrock, and by the time its settlement and tilt became public in 2016 the cheapest moment to fix the problem had long passed.

Recall

Q. What is downdrag?

A. Added downward load on a pile from a soil layer that settles around it after installation, so the soil hangs on the pile instead of supporting it.

Q. What is dewatering, and why does it affect neighbours?

A. Pumping groundwater down to keep an excavation dry. Lowering the water table increases the effective stress in the soil around it, which can cause soft layers under nearby buildings to consolidate and settle.

Q. What is a structural peer review?

A. An independent engineer's review of the structural design, its assumptions and its analysis, commissioned to catch errors and challenge judgment before construction.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman joins me because this case is a foundation story told in money and reputation. Nobody died. The building did not fall. Yet a foundation decision made early produced years of claims, a long dispute over who was to blame, a damaged asset for every owner in the building, and a repair that was itself difficult. I will keep to facts I am confident of and stay away from precise figures where reports differed.

1. Timeline

The tower was designed in the early 2000s and completed in 2009 on a concrete mat supported by concrete friction piles that ended in a dense sand layer, not in the bedrock that lay much deeper. Settlement greater than predicted was observed during and after construction. In 2016 it became public that the building had settled roughly 16 inches and was tilting, with the tilt later reported to have grown. Lawsuits followed among homeowners, the developer, the transit authority building a large transit centre next door, and others. A global settlement was reached around 2020. A retrofit adding piles to bedrock along part of the perimeter began, was paused in 2021 after it was found to be causing additional settlement during the work, and was later resumed in a revised form.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions mattered most. Ending the piles in the sand layer rather than taking them to bedrock, a choice that saved cost and was argued at the time to be adequate. Accepting the settlement predictions on which that choice depended. And, once settlement exceeded prediction, the pace and openness of the response to owners and buyers.

3. Assumptions

The design assumed that the deep clay layers beneath the sand would compress by a predictable and acceptable amount under the building's weight. It assumed, implicitly, that conditions around the site would stay broadly as they were. The developer later argued that the excavation and dewatering for the neighbouring transit centre changed those conditions. The transit authority argued that the tower's own foundation was the cause. That dispute matters less for your purposes than the lesson under it: a foundation that relies on the long-term behaviour of compressible soil is relying on assumptions about the soil and about everything that will happen around it for decades.

4. Incentives

Every party had a reason to want the cheaper foundation to be adequate. A foundation to bedrock costs more and takes longer. A developer selling units recovers the saving at sale and does not own the long-term risk once the units are sold. Engineers face pressure to find the design that works within budget. None of this means anyone acted in bad faith. It means the incentive to look hard at the downside was weak, and that is exactly when an independent review earns its fee.

Say that out loud now.

5. Warning signs ignored

Settlement measured during construction was ahead of prediction. A building that is already settling faster than designed while it is being built is giving you its most important piece of data, and the time to act on it is before occupancy and sale, not after. The public disclosure came years after completion. Whatever was known internally, the gap between the first evidence and the public response is where trust was lost.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the foundation design itself, once the mat was cast over the piles. After that, every fix meant working beneath or beside an occupied, heavy, already-tilting building, where new piles can themselves disturb the soil. The paused retrofit showed the problem exactly: the cure carried its own settlement risk. Changing a foundation before it is built costs money. Changing it after costs money, time, risk and reputation together.

7. Root cause

The root cause was a foundation whose performance depended on long-term consolidation of deep clay and on the stability of its surroundings, without a margin or a monitoring and response plan proportionate to that dependence. The trigger may be disputed. The vulnerability was designed in.

The developer's lens

Roman's view for you, Mr Shabazz: you will not design piles, but you will approve the foundation strategy and the budget behind it. When the cheaper option relies on predictions about compressible soil, insist on three things. An independent geotechnical peer review of the settlement prediction, with its range, not just its best estimate. A settlement monitoring plan with survey points read during and after construction, and written action triggers. And a clear view of what neighbours are planning, because their excavation and dewatering can change your ground.

What the record should have looked like

Ford's reconstruction, Mr Shabazz, of the evidence an owner should demand on any building that rests on compressible soil, whatever its height. Before design is frozen: a settlement prediction stated as a range, with the assumptions behind it written down, and an independent review that says whether the margin is adequate. During construction: survey points on the foundation and on columns, read on a fixed schedule, plotted against the predicted curve, and distributed to the owner, the engineers and the lender. In the contract: action triggers, meaning settlement values at which work pauses for an engineering review, and a named person who must act when a trigger is crossed. Around the site: a register of neighbouring works, especially excavations and dewatering, with the right to ask for their monitoring data.

None of that is exotic. It is a few survey visits a month, one review fee and some contract language. Compare it with what followed in this case: years of litigation, a retrofit that itself had to be paused, and a building whose name became shorthand for settlement. The asymmetry is the lesson. The cost of evidence is small and certain. The cost of not having it is large and arrives late.

Roman adds one point for lenders and buyers. When you sell units or refinance, the other side's engineer will ask for exactly this history. A clean monitoring record that tracks the prediction is an asset you can hand over. A record that starts after a problem became public is a liability, because it shows that nobody was watching when it mattered. Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineer and a licensed land surveyor for the monitoring programme.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that the foundation saving is booked by the developer while the settlement risk is carried by future owners, and that this mismatch quietly lowers everyone's scrutiny. The control is to treat long-term settlement as an owner risk you keep, review and monitor, whatever your exit plan.

The beginner's mistake

Reading the settlement figure in the report as a fact. It is a prediction with a range. Ask for the range, the assumptions behind it and the observation that would prove it wrong.

Callback

In Week 2, Kema taught the pre-mortem: imagine the project has failed and ask why. Run it on any foundation that rests on compressible soil, and the first answer is almost always settlement larger than predicted. That single question, asked early, is cheap.

Recap

A defensible foundation saving rested on predictions of deep clay settlement. Settlement exceeded prediction, causes were disputed, claims and a difficult retrofit followed. The vulnerability was built in when the mat was cast. Rule 111 makes long-term settlement an owner risk that is reviewed, monitored and acted on.

Next: Roman, on The Money: who pays when piles run long.
checklist: I ask whether the cheaper foundation relies on predicted long-term settlement of compressible soil.
I commission an independent geotechnical peer review of any such prediction.
I ask for the settlement range, not just the best estimate.
I require settlement monitoring points read during and after construction.
Monitoring has written action triggers and a named person who must act.
I find out what neighbours plan to excavate or dewater near my site.
I treat settlement ahead of prediction during construction as a stop-and-review signal.
Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineer, with independent peer review.
head: Field checklist
speak: The Millennium Tower in San Francisco was completed in 2009 on friction piles that ended in dense sand rather than bedrock. In 2016 it became public that it had settled roughly 16 inches and was tilting. Lawsuits followed, the causes were disputed between the tower and the transit project next door, and a perimeter retrofit was paused in 2021 because the repair itself caused settlement. The root cause was a foundation whose performance depended on long-term clay consolidation and stable surroundings, without margin or a monitoring and response plan to match. The saving was booked early; the risk was carried by later owners. Rule 111: when a foundation depends on predicted long-term settlement, get an independent review of the range, monitor settlement during and after construction against written triggers, and act before occupancy, not after.
terms: Friction pile — a pile that carries most of its load through skin friction along its length rather than bearing on rock at its tip.
Consolidation — the slow settlement of a saturated clay as water is squeezed out under a new load.
Settlement monitoring — repeated survey of fixed points on a building to measure how far and how evenly it moves down over time.

hostile.q: Your foundation ends in sand above deep clay to save money. Why should I lend against a building that could settle like Millennium Tower?
hostile.a: Because I am not asking you to trust the prediction. The settlement estimate has been peer reviewed by an independent geotechnical engineer, and I will give you the range, not only the best case. Survey points go on the mat and the columns from the first pour, readings are reported monthly to you and to me, and the contract sets triggers: past a set value we stop and review the design before more load goes on. I have also checked the neighbours' plans for excavation and dewatering. If the review had said the margin was thin, I would have taken the piles deeper and absorbed the cost.

rule: Rule 111: When a foundation depends on predicted long-term settlement, get an independent review of the full settlement range, monitor movement during and after construction against written triggers, and act on the first evidence before occupancy and sale.

title: Who Pays When Piles Run Long
summary: Pile length is the most uncertain quantity in the early budget, and the contract decides who carries that uncertainty. Unit rates, quantity ranges and a foundation contingency turn an open-ended risk into a priced one. The cost of long piles is not only the extra feet: it is the delay, the interest carry and the lender's view of your balance.
body:
Long piles cost you three times: once for the extra length, once for the delay to every trade behind them, and once in the interest you pay while the building waits, so the contract that prices pile length is really a contract about your schedule and your loan.

Recall

Q. What are the two ways a pile carries load?

A. Skin friction along its sides and end bearing at its tip, added together and divided by a factor of safety to give an allowable load.

Q. What is a temporary works design?

A. The engineered design of things built to support construction and then removed, such as shoring, excavation support, crane bases and falsework, which needs its own engineer and checks.

Q. What is a transfer floor?

A. A heavy floor structure that collects loads from columns above and redirects them to columns or walls in a different layout below, often at a podium.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the foundation contract is signed before anyone has seen the ground under most of the building. The borings are a sample. The design length is a prediction from that sample. That makes pile length one of the few big budget lines whose quantity, not just its price, is genuinely unknown on the day you commit. How you allocate that unknown decides whether a bad surprise is a priced adjustment or a dispute.

Three ways to buy piles

In plain English: you can pay a fixed price for the whole foundation, pay a rate for every foot actually installed, or mix the two.

A lump sum asks the contractor to price the risk of length. A careful contractor adds a premium for it, and a careless one under-prices it and then looks for a way out through a claim. A unit-price arrangement pays an agreed rate per foot, per pile or per load test, so the owner carries the quantity risk but pays only for what is installed. The common middle path is a schedule of unit rates with an estimated quantity and an agreed range, sometimes with rates that change if the quantity moves outside the range, because mobilisation and fixed costs are spread over fewer or more feet. Those mechanisms are commercial practice, negotiated contract by contract, not standards.

Pair any of these with the differing site conditions clause in your contract form. That clause, found in many standard forms, generally lets a contractor claim time and cost when the ground differs materially from what the contract documents indicated, or from what is ordinarily encountered. Read your actual form, because the wording and its notice requirements vary. Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer.

Worked example: pricing the length risk

Hypothetical round numbers. A site needs 200 piles. The design length is 60 feet, so the base quantity is 12,000 feet. The installed rate, including concrete, steel and labour, is 100 dollars per foot, giving a base cost of 1,200,000 dollars. Add 300,000 dollars for mobilisation, test piles and load testing: a foundation budget of 1,500,000 dollars.

Now the indicator piles show the competent layer is deeper, and the confirmed length is 75 feet. Quantity becomes 15,000 feet, an extra 3,000 feet at 100 dollars, which is 300,000 dollars more. That is a 20 percent increase on the foundation line, but only a small share of a 30,000,000 dollar project. The length alone is survivable.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example: the cost you do not see on the invoice

The extra length also takes time. Suppose the rig installs 8 piles a day at 60 feet and only 6 a day at 75 feet. At 8 a day, 200 piles take 25 working days. At 6 a day, they take about 34. Nine extra working days is roughly two calendar weeks. Every trade after the piles moves those two weeks, because foundations sit on the critical path, the sequence of work with no float that sets the finish date.

Two weeks of delay on the whole project costs more than two weeks of the pile rig. Suppose general conditions, meaning site staff, offices, cranes and insurance, run 60,000 dollars a week, and that interest on the drawn loan is small this early, say 10,000 dollars a week. Two weeks costs about 140,000 dollars, nearly half the extra length cost again. Later in the project, with the loan heavily drawn, the same two weeks would cost far more in interest. That is why the best moment for a foundation surprise is before production, during the test programme.

How the lender reads it

The lender's monitor sees two things: the foundation line moving, and the schedule moving. Both feed the in-balance test, which asks whether undisbursed loan plus remaining equity still covers the cost to complete. A foundation contingency, a reserve held specifically for pile length and ground risk and sized to the range the borings support, lets you absorb the 440,000 dollars of this example without going out of balance. Without it, the surplus comes from the general contingency, which you need for the rest of the building.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet: foundation risk arrives before the lender has advanced much, which means early overruns are often funded by equity, and if you have guaranteed cost overruns, by you. Keep the foundation contingency inside the project rather than relying on your own liquidity to cover it. Your liquidity floor, the cash you never commit, is not a project contingency. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal guarantee or funding decision.

Pricing the test programme honestly

Some owners see the test programme as a cost to trim. Run the numbers the other way, Mr Shabazz. In the hypothetical above, indicator piles and load tests cost perhaps 100,000 dollars of the 300,000 dollar allowance. What they buy is the right to commit to production with a known length. Without them, the first evidence of a long design might come from dynamic tests halfway through production, by which time some caps are poured over short piles. Remediating a single cap, with added piles drilled through or beside it and a thicker or larger cap, can cost several times one indicator pile, and the delay sits right on the critical path.

A practical way to frame it for a partner: the test programme is an option. You pay a small, known premium to learn the ground before you commit the large, uncertain spend. If the ground matches the borings, the option expires unused, and you have confirmed your budget. If it does not, the option pays out many times over. Priced that way, cutting the test programme to save money is selling an insurance policy you are about to need.

Write that framing into your foundation budget memo, Mr Shabazz, so that a partner or a lender reading it sees the test programme as a deliberate purchase rather than an overhead. Name its cost, its duration, the decision it unlocks and the date that decision is due. A line item with a stated purpose is much harder to cut in a value engineering session than a line called testing.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a lump-sum foundation contract priced too low, which converts honest ground uncertainty into a claim fight at the worst moment. The control is to buy length on unit rates with a range, fund a foundation contingency, and complete the test programme before production starts.

The beginner's mistake

Costing a deeper foundation as extra feet times rate and stopping there. The delay and the interest carry are part of the price.

Callback

In Week 51, Quincy and Nadia taught contingency structure: design, escalation and construction contingency held separately so each can be watched. A foundation contingency is the same idea applied to the most uncertain quantity on the job, and it should be reported on its own line.

Recap

Pile length is an unknown quantity at contract. Lump sums price that risk with a premium; unit rates with a range let the owner carry it at known cost. Long piles add length, delay and interest. A foundation contingency keeps the loan in balance.

Next: Ivo, on The Rules: the code, testing standards and records that govern deep foundations.
checklist: I know whether my foundation contract is lump sum, unit price or a hybrid.
Unit rates, the estimated quantity and the agreed range are written into the contract.
I have read the differing site conditions clause and its notice requirements.
I hold a foundation contingency sized to the length range the borings support.
I cost a deeper foundation with delay and interest, not only extra feet.
The test programme finishes before production piling begins.
I report foundation contingency to the lender's monitor on its own line.
Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer and quantity surveyor.
head: Field checklist
speak: Pile length is one of the few big budget lines whose quantity is unknown when I sign. A lump sum makes the contractor price that risk with a premium, or under-price it and claim later. Unit rates with an agreed quantity range let me carry it at a known price. In a hypothetical case, 200 piles going from 60 to 75 feet at 100 dollars a foot add 300,000 dollars. But the rig slows, the critical path moves about two weeks, and general conditions plus interest add roughly 140,000 more. So long piles cost length, delay and interest. I hold a foundation contingency sized to the range the borings support, report it to the lender separately, and finish the test programme before production starts, because that is the cheapest moment to be surprised.
terms: Unit-price contract — a contract that pays an agreed rate for each unit of work actually installed, so the owner carries the quantity risk.
Differing site conditions clause — a contract term that can give the contractor time and money when the ground materially differs from what the documents indicated.
Foundation contingency — a budget reserve held specifically for pile length and ground risk, reported separately from general contingency.

hostile.q: I'm the contractor. The borings were thin. Give me a lump sum price for the piles and I'll guarantee the number.
hostile.a: I would rather not buy your guarantee, because I would be paying a premium for a risk I can measure more cheaply myself. Price unit rates per foot, per pile and per load test, against an estimated quantity and an agreed range, with an adjusted rate outside the range. We install indicator piles first, and the geotechnical engineer confirms length and criteria before production. That way you are paid for what you install, I pay only for what the ground needs, and neither of us spends the job arguing about who knew what.

title: The Rules Under the Ground: Code, Testing and the Pile Record
summary: The building code requires a geotechnical investigation, governs how deep foundations are designed and installed, and calls for special inspection of the work. ASTM standards define how piles are load tested and checked for integrity. The pile record is the evidence that ties every installed pile to those rules.
body:
The code tells you that piles must be designed from a real investigation and inspected while they go in, the testing standards tell you how capacity and integrity are proven, and the pile record is the document that shows each pile met both.

Recall

Q. What does unit pricing do to the allocation of pile length risk?

A. It puts the quantity risk on the owner, who pays an agreed rate for each foot actually installed, instead of paying the contractor a premium to carry it in a lump sum.

Q. What is compaction testing in shallow foundation work?

A. Field tests of placed fill or subgrade, such as density tests, checked against a specified percentage of a laboratory maximum density, to confirm the ground was compacted as designed.

Q. What is commissioning intent in design management?

A. The owner's written statement of how building systems must perform, set early in design so that later testing has a defined target.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, deep foundations are where the code reaches below the visible building. You need to know what the rules require so you can see whether the contract, the inspection plan and the records satisfy them, and so you can spot when a schedule-driven decision quietly skips one. You do not need to quote section numbers. You need to know where to look and who must sign.

What the building code requires

In plain English: the code says a qualified engineer must investigate the ground, design the foundation for it, and an independent inspector must watch the foundation go in.

The International Building Code, the model code most American jurisdictions adopt with local amendments, has a chapter on soils and foundations and a chapter on special inspections. The foundation chapter addresses when a geotechnical investigation is required, what it must report, and the design and installation of deep foundations, including allowable capacities, load testing in certain cases, and spacing and splicing of piles. The special inspection chapter requires that certain work, deep foundations among it, be inspected by qualified special inspectors engaged on behalf of the owner rather than the contractor. Verify against the current adopted edition and local amendments before relying on any specific provision.

The practical meaning: the owner hires the special inspector. That independence is the point. An inspector paid by the installer is an inspector with a conflict.

How capacity and integrity are proven

ASTM International publishes the test methods. ASTM D1143 covers static axial compressive load testing, in which a pile is loaded with jacks against a reaction frame or dead weight and its movement measured. ASTM D4945 covers high-strain dynamic testing, in which sensors on the pile record strain and acceleration under hammer blows and a signal-matching analysis estimates capacity. For drilled shafts, ASTM D6760 covers crosshole sonic logging, which sends ultrasonic pulses between tubes cast into the shaft to find voids or soft concrete, and ASTM D5882 covers low-strain integrity testing. Confirm the current edition of each standard and which ones your specification calls up.

Applied example, hypothetical. A project specifies 2 static load tests to twice the design load on indicator piles, dynamic testing on 5 percent of production piles, and crosshole sonic logging on every drilled shaft. On 200 driven piles, that is 2 static tests and 10 dynamic tests. If a dynamic test shows a production pile well short of its required capacity, the specification should already say what happens next: the engineer evaluates, and the remedy might be redriving, an added pile, or a redesigned cap. The time to agree that path is before the first pile, not during the dispute.

Say that out loud now.

The pile record

The pile record is the installation log for each pile: its identifier and location, date, type and dimensions, ground and tip elevation, equipment used, and the data that proves it met the criteria. For a driven pile, that is the blow count per foot and the final set, meaning penetration per blow at the end of driving. For a drilled shaft, it is the depth, the bottom inspection, the concrete volume placed against the theoretical volume, and the integrity test result. For an augercast pile, it is the rig's monitoring printout of grout volume against depth.

Worked example, hypothetical. A drilled shaft of 3 feet diameter and 50 feet length has a theoretical volume of about 353 cubic feet, which is roughly 13 cubic yards. The record shows 11 cubic yards placed. Less concrete than the hole should hold is a red flag for a collapse or soil inclusion that narrowed the shaft. More than about 10 to 20 percent over can mean an over-break or a cavity. The inspector should flag the 11 cubic yards the same day, before the next shaft is drilled. That threshold is a project specification choice, not a code value.

Who must sign

The geotechnical engineer sets the installation criteria. The structural engineer of record sizes the caps and the loads. The special inspector observes and records. The contractor installs and logs. Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineer and structural engineer of record, with the special inspector's reports filed with the building department as the jurisdiction requires.

Two Systems

Canada, in concept: a national model building code is adopted with modifications by provinces and territories, and foundation design typically draws on national code requirements and engineering practice, with field review by the engineers of record. Guyana, in concept: building approvals run through national and local authorities, and foundation design on the soft coastal clays commonly relies on piles, with practice drawing on regional and international standards. Treat both descriptions as conceptual and verify against primary source.

When the ground differs from the contract

The rules above govern the engineering. A second set governs the money when the ground surprises everyone, and you met it on Day 3: the differing site conditions clause. Two points sit at the boundary between code and contract. First, the contract documents usually include, or reference, the geotechnical report. How they do so matters. If the report is listed as information only, a contractor may argue it could not rely on it; if it is a contract document, the contractor may argue it was entitled to rely on every boring. Ask your lawyer which your form does and whether that is what you want.

Second, the claim usually depends on notice. Many forms require the contractor to give written notice promptly, often before disturbing the condition, so the owner can see it. Your pile records and the inspector's daily reports are the evidence both sides will use to decide whether the ground really differed. That is another reason the records must be made on the day and kept by someone independent. Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer.

One practical habit closes the loop. Keep the geotechnical report, the specification, the test reports, the pile records and the non-conformance file in one indexed folder that you control, not only on the contractor's server. When a question comes years later, from a buyer, an insurer or a court, the owner who can produce that folder in an hour holds the strongest position in the room.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a pile that fails its criteria and is quietly accepted to keep the rig moving. The control is a written non-conformance procedure: any pile outside criteria is logged, reported to the geotechnical engineer and resolved in writing before the cap over it is poured.

The beginner's mistake

Letting the piling contractor hire the inspector or the testing firm to save a step. Independence is the whole value of inspection.

Callback

In Week 82, Vera taught that contemporaneous records, made at the time, beat recollection in every dispute. The pile record is the purest example in construction. It cannot be re-created later, because the pile is buried. If it is not written on the day, it does not exist.

Recap

The building code requires investigation, design and special inspection of deep foundations, verified against the adopted edition. ASTM methods prove capacity and integrity. The pile record ties each pile to its criteria. The owner hires the inspector.

Next: Greta, on The Numbers: sizing a pile group with downdrag, step by step.
checklist: I know which edition of the building code and local amendments apply.
The geotechnical investigation meets the code's reporting requirements.
I, the owner, engage the special inspector for deep foundations.
The specification names the load test and integrity test standards and frequencies.
There is a written procedure for any pile that fails its criteria.
Every pile has a record completed and signed on the day it is installed.
No pile cap is poured over a pile with an unresolved non-conformance.
Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineer, structural engineer of record and special inspector.
head: Field checklist
speak: The building code requires a geotechnical investigation, governs deep foundation design and installation, and calls for special inspection, with the owner engaging the inspector so there is no conflict. I verify every provision against the adopted edition. ASTM test methods prove the work: static load tests, high-strain dynamic tests, and for drilled shafts, crosshole sonic logging and low-strain integrity tests. The pile record ties each pile to its criteria: blow count and final set for a driven pile, depth, bottom inspection and concrete volume for a drilled shaft. In a hypothetical case, a shaft that should hold 13 cubic yards took only 11, which flags a possible collapse and must be resolved before the next shaft. Any pile outside criteria is logged and settled in writing before its cap is poured.
terms: Special inspection — inspection of specified critical work by a qualified inspector engaged for the owner, required by the building code.
Final set — the penetration of a driven pile per hammer blow at the end of driving, used as an acceptance criterion.
Crosshole sonic logging — an integrity test that sends ultrasonic pulses between tubes cast in a drilled shaft to detect voids or poor concrete.

hostile.q: I'm the building official. Show me that the piles under this cap meet the design.
hostile.a: Here are the pile records for each of the 8 piles under that cap, signed on the day of installation by the special inspector we engaged as owner. Each shows tip elevation and final set against the criteria the geotechnical engineer issued after the indicator pile load tests, and those test reports are attached. One pile was short of criteria; here is the non-conformance report, the engineer's written evaluation and the redrive record that closed it before the cap was poured.

title: Sizing a Pile Group, With Downdrag, Step by Step
summary: A worked calculation in hypothetical round numbers: compute one pile's ultimate capacity from friction and end bearing, apply a factor of safety, account for downdrag from a settling layer, and count the piles a column needs. Then see how a deeper design changes the count and the cost.
body:
The number of piles under a column is not a guess and not a quote: it falls out of five steps you can check yourself, and the step most often skipped, downdrag, is the one that changes the answer most.

Recall

Q. What does ASTM D4945 cover?

A. High-strain dynamic testing of piles: sensors record strain and acceleration under hammer blows, and a signal-matching analysis estimates capacity. Confirm the current edition.

Q. What is ground improvement under a shallow foundation?

A. Treating weak soil so it can carry a footing or mat, for example by compaction, preloading or rigid inclusions, instead of carrying the load past it with piles.

Q. What does ASCE 7 provide?

A. The minimum design loads for buildings and other structures in American practice, including dead, live, wind, snow and earthquake loads and how they combine.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will never sign a foundation calculation, but you will read foundation budgets, value engineering proposals and change orders. If you can rebuild the pile count in five steps, you can see whether a proposal to shorten piles or drop a few per cap is a real saving or a hidden risk. All numbers here are hypothetical round figures in American units. A kip is 1,000 pounds. Ksf means kips per square foot.

Step 1: the pile's geometry

The pile is an 18-inch square precast concrete pile, 60 feet long. The perimeter is 4 sides times 1.5 feet, which is 6 feet. The tip area is 1.5 times 1.5, which is 2.25 square feet. Side area per foot of length is the perimeter: 6 square feet per foot.

Step 2: ultimate capacity

The soil profile, from the geotechnical report, is 20 feet of soft clay over 40 feet of dense sand, with the tip in the sand. The engineer gives an average unit skin friction of 1.2 ksf in the sand and an end bearing of 80 ksf at the tip. Ignore the clay for now.

Skin friction in the sand: 6 square feet per foot, times 40 feet, times 1.2 ksf, equals 288 kips. End bearing: 2.25 square feet times 80 ksf equals 180 kips. Ultimate capacity is 288 plus 180, which is 468 kips.

Step 3: allowable capacity

The engineer applies a factor of safety of 2.0, justified by the planned load testing. Allowable capacity is 468 divided by 2.0, which is 234 kips per pile. The factor depends on the method, the code and the testing; it is the engineer's choice to justify, not yours.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: downdrag

Now the complication. Site grading places 6 feet of new fill over the soft clay, and the clay will consolidate under it for years. As it settles, it drags on the upper 20 feet of each pile. The engineer estimates negative skin friction of 0.4 ksf in that layer.

Drag load: 6 square feet per foot times 20 feet times 0.4 ksf equals 48 kips per pile. This is an added downward load. One common way to treat it, and the engineer decides the method, is to subtract it from what the pile can carry for the building: 234 minus 48 leaves 186 kips available per pile for the column. Downdrag has cut usable capacity by about 20 percent.

Step 5: count the piles

The column delivers 1,800 kips of service load to its cap, from the structural engineer's load takedown. The cap itself, a thick block of reinforced concrete, weighs about 90 kips. Total load to the piles is 1,890 kips.

Without downdrag: 1,890 divided by 234 is 8.08, so 9 piles. With downdrag: 1,890 divided by 186 is 10.16, so 11 piles. Two extra piles under one column. If the building has 40 similar columns, that is 80 extra piles. A designer who missed downdrag would have under-provided by about a fifth of the piles on the job.

Worked example two: the deeper alternative

Suppose instead the piles are lengthened to 75 feet, gaining 15 more feet in the sand. Added friction: 6 times 15 times 1.2 equals 108 kips. Assume end bearing stays at 180 kips. Ultimate becomes 288 plus 108 plus 180, which is 576 kips. Allowable at a factor of 2.0 is 288 kips. Less 48 kips of downdrag leaves 240 kips. Piles per column: 1,890 divided by 240 is 7.9, so 8 piles.

Compare the two options per column. Option A: 11 piles at 60 feet is 660 feet. Option B: 8 piles at 75 feet is 600 feet. Option B uses less pile length and needs a smaller cap, because fewer piles fit in less area. At a hypothetical 100 dollars per foot, the length saving is 6,000 dollars per column, or 240,000 dollars across 40 columns, before the cap saving. That depends on the rig being able to install 75-foot piles at a sensible rate, which the test programme would confirm.

What the numbers do not tell you

Pile groups behave differently from single piles: piles close together can share stressed soil and carry less in total than the sum of individuals, and a group in clay may settle more than one pile. The engineer applies group effects and checks group settlement. Lateral loads from wind and earthquake also act on piles. This calculation is a reader's check, not a design. Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineer and structural engineer of record.

Turning the calculation into a budget line

Mr Shabazz, carry the numbers one step further, into money. Option A, 11 piles of 60 feet per column across 40 columns, is 440 piles and 26,400 feet. Option B, 8 piles of 75 feet, is 320 piles and 24,000 feet. At a hypothetical 100 dollars per foot, Option A costs 2,640,000 dollars of pile and Option B 2,400,000 dollars, before caps. Caps follow pile count: a cap for 11 piles is larger and holds more concrete and reinforcing than a cap for 8. If each smaller cap saves a hypothetical 5,000 dollars, that is another 200,000 dollars across 40 columns.

Now check the schedule. Option B has 120 fewer piles to set up and install, though each takes longer to drive. If the rig installs 8 short piles a day or 6 long ones, Option A takes 55 working days and Option B about 53. Close enough to call even. The decision therefore turns on cost and on whether the test programme confirms that 75-foot piles reach the capacity assumed. That is the right shape for an owner decision: a clear saving, a neutral schedule, and one engineering question that a test can answer.

Last, write the comparison on one page for the decision log: Option A and Option B, total pile length, cap concrete, schedule days, cost, and the one test result that would change the answer. A one-page comparison lets a partner, a lender or your future self understand in two minutes why you chose as you did. It also makes the question you must ask the geotechnical engineer explicit, which is half of getting a straight answer to it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a value engineering proposal that cuts pile count using an allowable capacity that never subtracted downdrag. The control is to ask, for any reduction, which capacity per pile is being used and whether drag load has been taken off it.

The beginner's mistake

Rounding down. Eight point oh eight piles is nine piles. Capacity is not a number you share among columns.

Callback

In Week 13, Sage taught estimate classes: early numbers carry wide ranges that narrow as design firms up. Pile counts follow the same pattern. A schematic count before downdrag is known is a wide-range estimate, and treating it as a firm number is the classic early-budget error.

Recap

Geometry gives perimeter and tip area. Friction plus end bearing gives ultimate capacity. A factor of safety gives allowable. Downdrag subtracts usable capacity. Total load divided by usable capacity, rounded up, gives the count. Longer piles can mean fewer piles and less total length.

Next: Greta, on The Room: the meeting after the first load test comes in low.
checklist: I can compute perimeter and tip area for the pile type proposed.
I know the unit friction and end bearing values the report gives, by layer.
I know the factor of safety and the testing that justifies it.
I have asked whether downdrag applies and how it is treated.
I check pile counts by rounding up, never down.
I compare options on total pile length and cap size, not pile count alone.
I ask about group effects and lateral load before accepting any count.
Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineer and structural engineer of record.
head: Field checklist
speak: To check a pile count I use five steps. Geometry: an 18-inch square pile has a 6-foot perimeter and a 2.25 square foot tip. Ultimate capacity: 40 feet in sand at 1.2 ksf gives 288 kips of friction, plus 180 kips of end bearing, for 468. Allowable at a factor of 2 is 234. Downdrag: 20 feet of settling clay at 0.4 ksf drags 48 kips, leaving 186 usable. Count: a column and cap totalling 1,890 kips need 9 piles without downdrag and 11 with it. Lengthening to 75 feet lifts usable capacity to 240 kips, so 8 piles, which uses less total length than 11 short ones. So I always ask whether downdrag was subtracted, I round up, and I compare options on total length and cap size.
terms: Ultimate capacity — the total load a pile can carry before the soil fails, from skin friction plus end bearing.
Allowable capacity — the ultimate capacity divided by a factor of safety, the load a pile is designed to carry in service.
Load takedown — the structural engineer's tally of the loads each column or wall delivers to the foundation.

hostile.q: I'm the value engineering consultant. We can cut each cap from 11 piles to 9 and save a lot. Will you approve it?
hostile.a: Not on the number alone. Nine piles works only if each carries 210 kips usable, and the design shows 186 after subtracting 48 kips of downdrag from the soft clay. If your proposal used the 234 kip figure without downdrag, it under-provides by two piles a cap. If instead you propose longer piles with fewer per cap, that may save length and cap concrete, and I will ask the geotechnical engineer to confirm it against the indicator test results before I approve anything.

title: The Meeting After the Load Test Comes In Low
summary: The first static load test on an indicator pile has moved more than the criteria allow. In the room are the piling contractor, the geotechnical engineer, the structural engineer, the general contractor and the lender's monitor, each with a different interest. The lesson is how to turn a bad result into a decision, without blame and without letting production start on an untested design.
body:
When a load test comes in low, the meeting is not about who is at fault, it is about one decision: what design will production piles follow, and what evidence will prove it, and your job is to hold the room to that decision until it is made in writing.

Recall

Q. Why can longer piles mean fewer piles?

A. Extra length in good soil adds skin friction, raising capacity per pile enough that fewer piles carry the same load, sometimes with less total pile length and a smaller cap.

Q. Who should engage the special inspector on deep foundations?

A. The owner, so that the inspector is independent of the contractor whose work is being inspected.

Q. What is earned value in cost control?

A. A method that compares the budgeted value of work actually completed with both the planned value and the actual cost, showing whether a project is behind schedule or over budget.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the first hard foundation fact usually arrives in a meeting, not a report. The rig is on site and costing money every day. Every party has a reason to want a quick answer that suits it. A weak owner leaves that meeting with production piling resuming on a hopeful design. A strong owner leaves with a written decision, a test to prove it and a price.

The scene

Hypothetical. The indicator pile, a 60-foot driven pile, was load tested to twice its 234 kip design load. At design load it settled more than the specification allowed, and it plunged before reaching twice design load. The piling contractor's superintendent wants to start production this week on the original design. The geotechnical engineer suspects the dense sand is thinner here than in the borings. The structural engineer is worried about the cap layouts. The general contractor is watching the schedule. The lender's monitor is taking notes.

The question behind the question

The superintendent says, "The test setup may have been off. Let's drive and sort it out on the dynamic tests." The question behind his question is: will I be paid for standing time while you decide, and will I be paid if piles get longer? Answer that directly and the argument about the test usually softens.

The general contractor asks, "How many days?" The question behind it is: who carries the delay? The monitor's silence asks: is the loan still in balance?

The lines to say

Open with the decision, not the problem. "We have one decision today: the design production piles will follow, and the evidence that will confirm it. We will not drive production piles until that is in writing from the geotechnical engineer."

To the superintendent: "Standing time is a fair question. Keep a daily record of the rig and crew on standby, and we will deal with it under the contract terms. Unit rates cover extra length, so longer piles are paid for. I am not asking you to carry the ground."

To the geotechnical engineer: "What would you need to recommend a revised length with confidence, and how quickly? A second indicator pile, dynamic testing during driving, another boring?" Then: "Give me the options with their time and their cost, and your recommendation."

To the monitor: "You will have the revised length, the cost and the schedule effect by the end of the week, with the cost-to-complete update."

Say that out loud now.

A worked decision

Hypothetical figures. The geotechnical engineer offers three options. Option one: drive production at 60 feet and rely on dynamic tests, zero days of delay but a real chance of discovering short piles under poured caps. Option two: install a second indicator pile at 75 feet with dynamic testing during driving and a static test, about 8 working days and 40,000 dollars, then set production criteria. Option three: add two borings first, then a second indicator, about 15 days and 70,000 dollars.

Weigh them. Option one's cost is not zero; it is a gamble on remediating piles under caps, which can mean added piles, enlarged caps and redesign, each far more expensive than 8 days. Option two answers the specific question the test raised. Option three answers more questions than you have. Choose option two, unless the engineer says the variability is site-wide, in which case option three. Write it down: the decision, the reason, who recommended it and the date. That is your owner decision log.

The lines never to say

"Whose fault is this?" Blame in the first meeting turns every party into a defendant, and defendants stop sharing information. Fault, if it matters, is for later and for the records.

"Just keep driving and we'll see." That sentence converts a design question into an installed defect.

"It's probably the test." Maybe it is. Then prove it with another test, not with a hope.

When to stay silent

After you ask the geotechnical engineer for options, stop. Do not fill the pause with your own guess about length. Engineers give better answers when the owner is not leading them toward the cheap one. Stay silent again after stating that production does not start until the criteria are in writing. Let the room absorb it.

Holding your state

A low test feels like a budget wound, and your body will want to hurry. Before the meeting, write the one decision you need on a card. Speak slower than the most anxious person in the room. If your voice rises, finish the sentence, pause, and lower it. If you need a breathing reset, take it in your vehicle while parked before you walk in, never while driving. Calm is a tool here: the room will match the owner.

After the meeting

The meeting is only half the work, Mr Shabazz. Within the day, send a short note to every party: the decision, the reason, the test that will confirm it, the dates, and how standby and extra length will be paid. Ask each party to reply if their understanding differs. That note does three things. It turns a conversation into a record. It prevents the version of events that each party will otherwise reconstruct later. And it gives the lender's monitor exactly what the monitor needs for the next report.

Then put the second indicator pile and its results on the critical path in the schedule, with a hold point before production. Check that the cost of the extra test and the standby is drawn from the foundation contingency and not hidden in general conditions, so the contingency report shows the truth. When the results arrive, call the same people back for a short meeting to accept the criteria in writing.

A final discipline: before you leave the site that day, walk to the rig and thank the crew for the clean test setup, whatever the result. The people running the rig will install every pile you depend on, and a foundation crew that feels blamed for a bad number has every reason to be less careful about the next record. Firmness on the decision and respect for the people doing the work are not in tension. They are both part of owning the job.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that schedule pressure restarts production before the design is proven. The control is a hold point in the contract: no production piling until the geotechnical engineer issues written criteria based on test results.

The beginner's mistake

Arguing about the test method with the contractor. You are not the expert in the room on load tests. Your job is to ask for options, weigh them in time and money, and decide.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught the hostile question technique: acknowledge, bridge, answer. The superintendent's challenge to the test is a hostile question. Acknowledge it, bridge to the decision, and answer with the evidence you will gather.

Recap

A low load test calls for one decision: the production design and the evidence behind it. Answer each party's real question: payment, delay, balance. Ask for options with time and cost, choose the one that answers the question raised, and record it. No production until the criteria are in writing.

Next: Kema, on Quiz and Recap: Week 111 review, deep foundations.
checklist: I open the meeting with the one decision required.
I state that production piling waits for written criteria.
I answer the contractor's real question about standby and length payment.
I ask the geotechnical engineer for options with time, cost and a recommendation.
I weigh the cost of remediating piles under poured caps, not just delay.
I record the decision, reason, recommender and date in the owner decision log.
I tell the lender's monitor when the cost-to-complete update will arrive.
Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineer.
head: Field checklist
speak: When a load test comes in low, I go into the room with one decision written on a card: what design will production piles follow, and what evidence will prove it. I say up front that no production pile is driven until the geotechnical engineer gives written criteria. I answer each party's real question: the contractor's is payment for standby and extra length, so I tell him to log standby and that unit rates cover length. The contractor's question about days is really about who carries delay. I ask the engineer for options with time, cost and a recommendation, then stay silent. In a hypothetical case, a second indicator pile costs about 8 days and 40,000 dollars, far cheaper than remediating short piles under poured caps. I record the decision in the owner decision log and give the lender's monitor a date for the updated cost to complete.
terms: Indicator pile — an early pile installed with the production rig and tested to confirm the design before production piling starts.
Hold point — a defined stage in the work beyond which the contractor may not proceed until a named party approves in writing.
Owner decision log — a dated record of each owner decision, its reason and who recommended it.

hostile.q: I'm the piling contractor. Every day you spend testing costs me a rig and a crew. Either let me drive or pay me now.
hostile.a: I understand the cost, and I am not asking you to carry it silently. Keep a daily standby record of rig and crew, signed by our inspector, and we will settle it under the contract terms. Extra length is covered by the unit rates. What I will not do is let production start on a design the first test did not support, because remediating short piles under poured caps would cost both of us far more than eight days. The second indicator pile starts as soon as you can mobilise it.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 111 Review: The Foundation You Cannot See
summary: Six questions on deep foundations, a recap of the week, a Red Pen drill on a hypothetical pile record and specification note with planted defects, and a two-minute boardroom drill with a model answer.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: a pile is a load path you cannot inspect after it is buried, so the design must be proven by tests before production, and every pile must carry a record made on the day.

Recall

Q. In a load test meeting, what is the one decision you must leave with?

A. The design production piles will follow and the evidence that will confirm it, written down by the geotechnical engineer.

Q. What is a survey control network on a site?

A. A set of fixed, surveyed reference points from which every building element is set out, checked and re-checked throughout construction.

Q. What does progressive collapse mean?

A. A failure in which the loss of one element spreads to others, so a local failure becomes a disproportionate one.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, if you can answer these six without notes, you can sit with a geotechnical engineer, a piling contractor and a lender's monitor and follow every number. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the two ways a pile carries load, and say which needs more movement to mobilise.

Answer: Skin friction along the shaft and end bearing at the tip. Friction mobilises with small movement; full end bearing needs more movement at the tip.

Question 2. What is downdrag, and what causes it?

Answer: Added downward load on a pile from a settling soil layer around it. It comes from fill over soft clay, a lowered water table, or soft soil still consolidating.

Question 3. What was the root cause in the Millennium Tower case?

Answer: A foundation that ended in sand above deep clay, whose performance depended on predicted long-term consolidation and stable surroundings, without margin or a monitoring and response plan to match. The trigger was disputed; the vulnerability was designed in.

Question 4. Why do long piles cost more than extra feet times rate?

Answer: Because they slow the rig and move the critical path, adding general conditions and interest carry. The extra feet are only one of three costs.

Question 5. Who engages the special inspector, and why?

Answer: The owner, so the inspector is independent of the contractor whose work is being inspected.

Question 6. A column and cap deliver 1,890 kips, and each pile has 186 kips usable after downdrag. How many piles?

Answer: 1,890 divided by 186 is 10.16, so 11 piles. Always round up.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Greta framed the pile as a hidden load path proven by tests. Ford and Roman took the Millennium Tower settlement through seven steps, giving Rule 111. Roman priced long piles as length, delay and interest. Ivo set out the code, the test standards and the pile record. Greta sized a pile group with downdrag. Greta ran the meeting after a low load test.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical pile record and specification note. Find the defects before reading on.

Pile record, Pile P-47, drilled shaft, 3 feet diameter. Design length 50 feet. Drilled to 46 feet, bottom judged acceptable by the drilling foreman. Concrete placed: 11 cubic yards. Crosshole sonic logging: to be done at the end of the job with the others. Inspector: engaged by the piling subcontractor. Note: cap C-12 over P-45 to P-48 may be poured Monday to hold the schedule. Specification note: production piling may begin once the indicator pile is installed.

The defects. First, the shaft stopped 4 feet short of design length with no engineer's approval recorded. Second, the bottom was accepted by the drilling foreman, not the geotechnical engineer or the special inspector. Third, 11 cubic yards against a theoretical volume of about 13 cubic yards for a 46-foot length is under-volume, a sign of possible collapse or inclusion, and it is not flagged. Fourth, integrity testing is deferred to the end of the job, so a defective shaft could be buried under a cap before anyone knows. Fifth, the inspector is engaged by the subcontractor, which destroys independence. Sixth, the cap is scheduled over a pile with open questions. Seventh, the specification lets production start once the indicator is installed, not once it is tested and criteria are issued.

The corrected version: the shaft depth is approved or the shaft is extended by the geotechnical engineer; the bottom is inspected by the special inspector, engaged by the owner; the volume shortfall is reported as a non-conformance; integrity testing is done before the cap is formed; and production starts only after test results and written criteria.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a partner who asks, "Why is the foundation line so uncertain, and how do we control it?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Where the upper soil is weak, piles carry the building down to ground that can hold it, through friction along their sides and bearing at their tips. The design length is a prediction from a few borings, so it is the most uncertain quantity in the early budget. We control it three ways. First, we test before we build: indicator piles are load tested and the engineer issues written criteria before production starts. Second, we buy length on unit rates with an agreed range and hold a foundation contingency, so extra length has a known price. Third, every pile gets a record on the day it goes in, checked by an inspector we hire, and nothing gets covered until it passes. We also check for downdrag and long-term settlement, because a foundation that depends on soft clay behaving well needs monitoring for years. Millennium Tower shows what happens when that is skipped."

Score your own answer. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you name testing before production, unit rates with a range and the pile record? Did you mention settlement? Did you finish inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

Self-test before you move on

Kema's check, Mr Shabazz. Without looking back, write three things on a card. One: the order of evidence on a deep foundation, from borings to indicator piles to load tests to written criteria to production to the pile record. Two: the three costs of long piles, which are length, delay and interest. Three: Rule 111 in your own words. If you can write all three in under two minutes, the week has landed. If one is missing, reread that day's lesson tonight and try again tomorrow morning. The point is not to memorise this week's numbers, which are hypothetical. It is to carry the sequence into every foundation meeting you will ever attend, so that you notice at once when a step is about to be skipped.

One more habit. Before the first foundation meeting on any real project, write down the question you most fear being asked, and the evidence that would answer it. If you cannot name the evidence, that is your first request to the team.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is covering a pile before its evidence is complete. The control is a rule: no cap over any pile with an open record, test or non-conformance.

The beginner's mistake

Remembering the pile types and forgetting the evidence. The types are easy; the records decide whether you can defend the building.

Callback

In Week 48, Marco taught the owner decision log as the backbone of governance. This week the log earned its keep twice: in the load test meeting and in any non-conformance, where a dated decision is the only defence later.

Recap

Piles carry load by friction and end bearing, proven by testing before production. Downdrag and long-term settlement must be found in design. Length risk is priced with unit rates and a contingency. Every pile has a day-of record checked by an owner's inspector.

hostile.q: I'm the buyer's engineer at sale. Show me why I should trust a foundation I can't see.
hostile.a: Because you do not have to trust it; you can audit it. Here are the indicator pile load test reports, the geotechnical engineer's written production criteria, and a signed record for every pile showing its tip elevation and acceptance data against those criteria. The special inspector was engaged by the owner, and every non-conformance has a report and a written resolution dated before its cap was poured. The settlement monitoring readings since completion are attached, plotted against the predicted range.
